Empirical Research Plan: U.S. Government-Spending Multipliers, 1947–2008

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Strategy: Instrumental-Variables Local Projections (IV-LP)

• Why IV?  Ordinary least squares is hopeless because government purchases are jointly
  determined with the state of the economy (reverse causality and automatic
  stabilizers).  
• Why external instruments?  Narrative “news” series about future military
  outlays (Ramey 2011) and professional-forecast errors are plausibly exogenous
  to contemporaneous business-cycle conditions yet strongly predictive of
  subsequent government-spending realizations.  
• Why local projections?  They deliver impulse-response functions and allow
  straightforward interaction with recession dummies, giving horizon-specific
  multipliers without imposing VAR restrictions.  

Hence the causal parameter is identified off exogenous forecast-error (news)
shocks, using 2SLS at each horizon h (Jordà, 2005) or a stacked-LP system
(Plagborg-Møller & Wolf, 2021).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment Variable  
 Tt ≡ Δĝt = “exogenous” change in real government purchases:  
 first-stage: Δgt = π Zt + controls + ut,  
 where Zt is the instrument (see below).  

Instruments (Zt)  
1. Ramey “military news” series (available 1939–2014).  
2. Forecast-error shocks: actual – SPF/Greenbook/RSQE forecast of government
   purchases 1- to 4-quarters ahead (take first PC of all available sources).  
   We use news only (positive or negative).  

Control Group / Counterfactual  
Dates in which Zt ≈ 0 serve as implicit control; IV delivers the average causal
response to a standardized, unanticipated spending shock.  

Treatment Timing  
Event date = quarter t in which the shock occurs.  Responses traced 0–16
quarters ahead.  

Business-Cycle Heterogeneity  
Define Recessiont = 1 if quarter t is inside an NBER recession, 0 otherwise.
Main specification interacts the shock with Recessiont.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Relevance:  Zt is strongly correlated with Δgt (F-stat > 10).  
 Plausible—the narrative/news series is by construction about future spending.

A2. Exclusion:  Conditional on controls, Zt affects output only through
 government purchases.  
 • Military-news shocks could affect uncertainty or geopolitical risk; we control
   for relative defense share and oil-price shocks to mitigate this channel.

A3. No Anticipation:  Private agents do not foresee Zt beyond what is already
 captured in published forecasts; otherwise the baseline would confound
 expectations.  Using forecast errors (rather than levels) makes this plausible.

A4. Linear, time-invariant impulse-responses within regime (recession/expansion).
 Local projections allow heterogeneous coefficients across regimes to relax
 this somewhat.

A5. Stable Unit Treatment Value (SUTVA) in the time-series sense: each shock is
 small relative to the economy so that overlapping dynamic effects are additive.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats & Mitigations
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Confounding Geopolitical Events  
 Military news often coincides with wars that also move oil prices,
 uncertainty, and sentiment.  
 • Add control vector Xt: oil-price growth, VXO implied-volatility index,
   Romer-Romer monetary-policy shocks, and defense-contract awards.  
 • Run sub-sample excluding Korean, Vietnam, and Gulf-War periods.

T2. Weak-Instrument Problem in Sub-samples  
 The military-news series is sparse in expansions.  
 • Report first-stage F-stats for full sample and subsamples.  
 • Combine instruments (news + forecast errors) to raise relevance.
 • Use LIML and Anderson-Rubin confidence sets as robustness.

T3. Finite-sample Bias / Small-T Inference  
 Quarterly aggregate series ⇒ only 248 observations.  
 • HAC Newey-West SEs with small-sample correction (Sun, 2022).  
 • Bootstrap (block length 8 quarters).  
 • Report median-unbiased estimates (Andrews & Stock, 2005).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# Required packages
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(fixest)        # fast 2SLS and HAC SEs
library(haven)         # if data in .dta
library(lpirfs)        # Local-projection helper
library(AER)           # ivreg for robustness
library(sandwich)
library(lmtest)

# 1. Load quarterly data -------------------------------------------------
macro   <- read_csv("macro_quarterly_1947_2008.csv")  # g, y, taxes, defl, etc.
spfcst  <- read_csv("spf_forecasts.csv")              # SPF vintages
green   <- read_csv("greenbook_forecasts.csv")
ramey   <- read_csv("ramey_military_news.csv")
nber    <- read_csv("nber_recessions.csv")

# 2. Construct variables --------------------------------------------------
data <- macro %>%
  mutate(date = yq(date)) %>%
  left_join(ramey,  by = "date") %>%
  left_join(nber,   by = "date") %>%
  # Growth rates (log diffs)
  mutate(dg    = 400* (log(real_g)  - lag(log(real_g))),    # annualized q-o-q
         dy    = 400* (log(real_gdp)- lag(log(real_gdp))),
         rec   = if_else(nber_recession == 1, 1, 0))

# Forecast errors (example SPF, 1-q ahead)
spf_fe <- spfcst %>%
  mutate(fe_g = log(actual_real_g) - log(spf_pred_g)) %>%
  select(date, fe_g)

data <- left_join(data, spf_fe, by = "date")

# Primary instrument: combine news and forecast error
data <- data %>%
  mutate(z = coalesce(ramey_news, 0) + coalesce(fe_g, 0))

# Lags/leads for LP
H <- 16   # horizons
for (h in 0:H){
  data <- data %>%
    mutate(!!paste0("dy_lead",h) := lead(dy, h))
}

# 3. Local projection loop -----------------------------------------------
results <- list()
for (h in 0:H){
  fml <- as.formula(paste0("dy_lead",h,
           " ~ 1 | (dg ~ z) + rec + dg*rec + dy + lag(dy,1:4)"))
  
  est <- feols(fml,
               data = data,
               vcov = ~ nw,
               stage = 2)
  
  results[[h+1]] <- est
}

# 4. Robustness: exclude war periods -------------------------------------
wars <- data %>% filter(date %within% interval(ymd("1950-06-01"), ymd("1953-07-31")) |
                         date %within% interval(ymd("1965-03-01"), ymd("1973-01-31")) |
                         date %within% interval(ymd("1990-08-01"), ymd("1991-02-28"))) %>%
                 pull(date)

data_nowar <- data %>% filter(!date %in% wars)

# Re-estimate h = 4 only as illustration
est_nowar <- feols(dy_lead4 ~ 1 | (dg ~ z) + rec + dg*rec + dy + lag(dy,1:4),
                   data = data_nowar,
                   vcov = ~nw)

summary(est_nowar)
```
Notes:  
1. `feols` syntax “y ~ 1 | (x ~ z)” performs 2SLS; add HAC via `vcov = ~nw`.  
2. Stacked LP (single regression for all horizons) is also possible; code keeps
   it simple.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Theory (New Keynesian with slack + ZLB) and previous narrative studies suggest:

• Peak multiplier (cumulative five-year dollar change in GDP per $1 change in G)
  ≈ 0.6–0.8 in expansions, ≈ 1.2–1.8 in recessions.  
• Defense shocks should yield larger multipliers (defense spending is more
  exogenous).  
• Government investment likely produces higher multipliers than consumption,
  though data are noisier.  
• Controlling for anticipated components will reduce the measured multiplier
  because some of the private-sector response occurs before spending is recorded.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV context)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Instrument relevance (F-stat > 10) ............ 1  
C2: Exclusion (no direct effect on Y) ............. 0.5  
C3: No anticipation / timing validity ............. 0.5  
C4: Correct functional form / dynamics ............ 1  
C5: Robust standard errors & inference ............ 1  

Total (out of 5) .................................. 4.0  

We judge exclusion and no-anticipation as partially, not fully, satisfied due to
possible war-related channels and imperfect foresight, but multiple robustness
checks mitigate these concerns.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
End of Plan
